questions.question: What is motor insurance and why is it important? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is motor insurance and why is it important?
  • ● What it is : Motor insurance is a policy that provides financial protection for vehicles against losses
  • from accidents, theft, or natural disasters.(1.5 Marks)
  • ● Why it is important : It covers repair costs and, crucially, covers third -party liability (damage
  • caused to others), which is mandatory by law in India. (1.5 Marks)

questions.question: Describe the evolution of life insurance during the colonial period in India. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the evolution of life insurance during the colonial period in India.
  • ● Life insurance began in 1818 with the Oriental Life Insurance Company, primarily for Europeans.
  • Indian lives were charged higher premiums. The first Indian company, Bombay Mutual Life
  • Assurance Society (1870), insured Indian lives at standard rates. (Full marks for mentioning the start,
  • discrimination, and the first Indian company). (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is principle of indemnity? Explain its main purpose. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is principle of indemnity? Explain its main purpose.
  • ● Principle :States that insurance should restore the insured to the same financial position they were
  • in before the loss, not allow them to profit. (1.5 Marks)
  • ● Purpose : To provide compensation for the actual loss and prevent insurance from being used for
  • profit or gambling. (1.5 Marks)

questions.question: Why fair distribution of surplus important? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Why fair distribution of surplus important?
  • ● Surplus is the profit of the insurer. Fair distribution is vital for "with-profit" policies, as this profit is
  • shared with policyholders as bonuses. It ensures transparency, delivers the promised returns, and
  • maintains customer trust. (3 Marks)

questions.question: In 'Proportional Reinsurance', how are premiums and losses shared between the insurer and reinsurer? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• In 'Proportional Reinsurance', how are premiums and losses shared between the insurer and
  • reinsurer?
  • ● The insurer (ceding company) and the reinsurer share premiums and losses in a fixed, pre-agreed
  • percentage. For example, in a 60% share, the reinsurer receives 60% of the premium and pays 60%
  • of the claims. (3 Marks)

questions.question: What is the first step a family must take when a person covered by a life insurance policy goes missing? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is the first step a family must take when a person covered by a life insurance policy goes
  • missing?
  • ● The very first step a family must take when a person covered by a life insurance policy goes missing
  • is to file a Missing Person's Report (First Information Report or FIR) with the local police. This
  • official report is the primary document required to initiate any legal or insurance process. It formally
  • documents the disappearance, which is essential as a person can generally only be legally presumed
  • dead after seven years from the date of this report. (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What two factors are used to categorise risks in the 2x2 Risk Management Matrix? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What two factors are used to categorise risks in the 2x2 Risk Management Matrix?
  • ● The two factors used to categorize risks in a 2x2 Risk Management Matrix are Risk Likelihood and
  • Risk Impact.
  • ● Risk Likelihood (or Frequency): This factor assesses how often or how probable it is that a specific
  • risk will actually happen (e.g., 'Rare', 'Possible', 'Frequent'). (1.5 Marks)
  • ● Risk Impact (or Severity): This factor measures the seriousness of the consequences or the damage
  • that would be caused if the risk occurred (e.g., 'Minor', 'Moderate', 'Catastrophic'). (1.5 Marks)

questions.question: What happens if an agent acts outside their authority? / [CO4] [3x10 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• What happens if an agent acts outside their authority?
  • ● The insurance company (principal) is generally not liable for acts outside the agent's actual authority.
  • However, the company may be liable if the agent acted within their apparent (perceived) authority.
  • The agent can be held personally liable for the breach. (3 Marks)

questions.question: Explain the structure and composition of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the structure and composition of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority
  • of India (IRDAI).
  • ● Structure : IRDAI is the statutory, independent regulatory body for the insurance industry in India,
  • headquartered in Hyderabad. Its role is to protect policyholders and regulate the industry. (2 Marks)
  • ● Composition : It is a 10-member body: one Chairperson, five full-time members, and four part-time
  • members, all appointed by the Government of India. (4 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the role and importance of the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC). / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the role and importance of the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC).
  • ● Role : Established in 1956 by nationalizing the sector. Its primary role was to spread life insurance
  • awareness across India, especially in rural areas, and to channel public savings into national
  • development. (3 Marks)
  • ● Importance : LIC is the largest insurer in India with a dominant market share. It has a vast agency
  • network, fosters a culture of savings, and is a major domestic institutional investor, significantly
  • contributing to the economy. (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain how age and health influencing life insurance. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how age and health influencing life insurance.
  • ● Influence of Age : Age is a primary risk factor. A younger person has lower mortality risk, so
  • premiums are lower. As age increases, the risk of death increases, leading to significantly higher
  • premiums for new policies. (3 Marks)
  • ● Influence of Health : Health is assessed via underwriting (medical history, habits like smoking). A
  • healthy person pays a standard premium. An individual with pre-existing conditions (e.g., diabetes)
  • or risky habits will be charged a higher premium (a "loading") or may be denied coverage. (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: LIC's Jeevan Akshay VI and New Jeevan Shanti are both pension plans. Explain the key difference in when you start receiving the pension from each? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• LIC's Jeevan Akshay VI and New Jeevan Shanti are both pension plans. Explain the key
  • difference in when you start receiving the pension from each?
  • ● Jeevan Akshay VI : This is an Immediate Annuity plan. The policyholder pays a single lump-sum
  • premium, and the pension (annuity) payments begin immediately (e.g., from the next month). (3
  • Marks)
  • ● New Jeevan Shanti : This is a Deferred Annuity plan. The policyholder pays a lump sum, but the
  • pension payments are deferred (postponed) for a chosen period (e.g., 1 to 20 years). This allows the
  • fund to grow, resulting in a higher pension amount later. (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is a Provident Fund (PF) and how does it work? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is a Provident Fund (PF) and how does it work?
  • ● What it is : A Provident Fund (like EPF) is a mandatory, long -term retirement savings scheme for
  • salaried employees in India. (2 Marks)
  • ● How it works : A fixed percentage of the employee's salary is deducted and contributed. The
  • employer makes a matching contribution. This accumulated amount earns a government -declared,
  • tax-free interest. The total corpus is paid out as a lump sum upon retirement. (4 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does a ULIP work? Where does your money go when you pay the premium? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• How does a ULIP work? Where does your money go when you pay the premium?
  • ● How it works : A ULIP (Unit Linked Insurance Plan) is a product that combines insurance (life
  • cover) and investment. (2 Marks)
  • ● Where money goes : When a premium is paid, a portion is deducted for charges (mortality charge
  • for life cover, admin charges). The remaining amount is invested in market-linked funds (e.g., equity,
  • debt) chosen by the policyholder, who bears the investment risk. (4 Marks)

questions.question: What is an Endowment Plan and how is it different from a Term Plan? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is an Endowment Plan and how is it different from a Term Plan?
  • ● Endowment Plan : This is a savings-oriented policy that provides a dual benefit: (1) A death benefit
  • to the nominee if the insured dies during the term, and (2) A maturity benefit (sum assured + bonuses)
  • to the policyholder if they survive the term. (3 Marks)
  • ● Difference : A Term Plan is a pure -risk policy; it only pays a death benefit and has no
  • maturity/survival value. Because of the savings component, Endowment Plan premiums are much
  • higher than Term Plan premiums for the same cover. (3 Marks)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

  • completely.

  • occupation, etc., that could affect the insurer's decision.
  • ○ Consequence (2 Marks): Failure to disclose (misrepresentation or non -disclosure) of a
